extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (community relations managers, corporate PR teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for designing, implementing, and evaluating community relations programs that are contingent on community structure (pluralism) and aimed at leaders of community-interest publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency on community pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations programs should be contingent upon the degree to which a community is more or less pluralistic; programs that work in less-pluralistic communities will not necessarily work in more-pluralistic communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess community characteristics (population size, ethnic diversity, absentee ownership, in-migration, economic diversity) and adapt tactics accordingly; e.g., expressive symbolic activities (parades, ceremonies) and press-agentry/publicity often work better in less-pluralistic communities, while two-way symmetric approaches are more appropriate in more-pluralistic communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations should be a two-way symmetric communication process (dialogue) rather than one-way or manipulative monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize interviewing community leaders, holding group dialogue sessions, and passing insights back to management. Two-way symmetric approaches are linked with better planning and outcomes in active teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize communication and message-retention objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The communication objective and message retention should be stressed over expecting attitude or behavior change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether community leaders understand and retain the organization's position on controversial/policy issues; recognize that attitude/behavior objectives are seldom achieved but communication and retention are realistic goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim community relations at community-interest-group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should be aimed at leaders of community-interest publics (constituencies) rather than simply trying to reach the community-at-large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and contact diverse leaders of important interest groups (consumerists, minorities, government, etc.) rather than relying only on business leaders or mass dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize instrumental over expressive participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumental (problem-solving) community participation projects are generally more appreciated and effective with community leaders than expressive symbolic activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design projects that address important community problems rather than only sponsoring symbolic activities (e.g., charity, parades) if the objective is community problem solving or leader appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek out diverse and nontraditional leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations personnel should proactively seek diverse community leaders who may represent constituencies that do not necessarily support the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include nontraditional influentials (minority leaders, consumer advocates, community activists) when interviewing and planning; avoid interviewing only businesspeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate about controversial topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations personnel should not avoid controversy; they should communicate about controversial or policy topics with community leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-ended questions to document what was discussed; controversial discussion can increase message retention even if it does not produce attitudinal support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel information from community to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and maintain mechanisms for channeling information (especially about controversial topics and community problems) back to organizational management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create feedback loops so that managers receive information from community relations reps and can consider policy or behavioral changes in response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect community relations to produce active support
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume community relations contact will produce active support or even passive acceptance of organizational positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic performance expectations: improved understanding and redirected negative behaviors are plausible outcomes, but active advocacy is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community relations to help solve important community problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat community relations as a mechanism to assist the organization in addressing and solving significant community problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor instrumental projects that contribute substantively to community problem solving and document the organization's contribution to priority problems as evaluated by community leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative research: know community structure and linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: Before planning, practitioners must know: the extent to which the community is pluralistic/centralized; the different kinds of community leaders; controversial issues/problems; and the organization's linkages with publics and other organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these domains to guide program objectives, target publics, and tactic selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community case method for formative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ intensive case-study methods (short-term fieldwork using observation, participation, role-playing, unstructured depth interviews, and content analysis) to gather information about community publics and issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers may spend 2–3 days in the community, conduct snowball interviews with influentials, observe events, attend meetings, and analyze local media coverage for issues relevant to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify publics using situational theory concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment and identify community publics by problem recognition, level of involvement, and perceived constraint (situational theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey and situational measures to distinguish active, constrained, fatalistic, and nonactive publics and to prioritize whom to target for communication and participation projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and evaluate activities (avoid only traditional tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective community relations teams plan and evaluate fewer, better-targeted activities rather than engaging in many easy/traditional events without planning or evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-support teams concentrate on interviews and dialogue sessions and evaluate outcomes; low-support teams tend to do open houses, films, civic ceremonies and do not evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure contacts with community leaders and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Track the number of local governmental officials and members of local publics (interest groups or constituencies) reporting contact with community relations representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use leader surveys to count contacts as a basic communication-output metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure discussions of controversial/policy issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of community leaders who report having discussed controversial or policy issues with community relations representatives (using open-end questions to capture topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gauges willingness to engage substantively and the depth of dialogue beyond general publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure message understanding/retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of community leaders who understand the organization's position on controversial or policy questions (message retention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific questions (from Chapter 9) to test recall and comprehension of organizational positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure information flow from publics to organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of community leaders who report giving information to community relations representatives about service or community problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect open-ended accounts of information provided to capture content and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure managerial receipt and action on information
rubrics_metrics.description: Track the number of organizational managers who report having received information about service or community problems from community relations representatives and the number who report making policy or behavior changes as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measures whether community intelligence is reaching decision-makers and producing organizational change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure negative behaviors and their targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of negative behaviors reported by community leaders and the percentage of those behaviors directed toward the organization versus through outside groups/agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing negative behaviors, and redirecting them toward the organization (so the organization can respond) rather than toward political channels, can be considered a program effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate community involvement projects by leader ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ratings by community leaders of the extent to which the organization helped solve the three most important community problems defined by each leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leader evaluations provide a direct assessment of instrumental project impact and community appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media and tactic expectations to community type
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate that media in less-pluralistic communities will reinforce the status quo and ignore conflict, producing more favorable publicity for expressive activities; in more-pluralistic communities media will report conflict and seek access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tactics with these media tendencies in mind—expect more favorable coverage from symbolic activities in less-pluralistic settings, but plan for media scrutiny in pluralistic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize absentee ownership effects on strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: When key businesspeople are representatives of absentee-owned corporations, the company’s community relations may emphasize expressive activities and not attempt local political control; involvement varies with corporate mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of corporate embeddedness in the community to determine whether to pursue instrumental projects or mainly expressive sponsorships; more immobile/locally embedded firms will tend to engage instrumentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect varied publics by issue type (consequential vs general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different publics arise from general community problems (urban renewal, taxes) versus organization-specific consequences (layoffs, construction); consequently, publics to target will differ by issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map publics to issues using situational indicators; do not assume the same publics are relevant across issue types.
